title: Communication-Friendly Area
strapline: A low-arousal talking corner with symbols and objects of reference, so every child has a way in — words or not.
intent: Children who don't yet use speech get real ways to communicate — pointing to a symbol, handing over an object, using a sign.
Children experience a calm, uncluttered space where the sound and visual load is low enough to actually listen and be heard.
Children learn that all communication counts here — a gesture, a photo, a single word are all met as if they'd made a speech.
Children build shared attention and turn-taking with an adult who slows right down and waits.
Children who are learning English or are pre-verbal find objects and pictures that carry meaning across any language.
implementation: Strip the corner back — muted colours, soft furnishing, no jangling background music, minimal wall clutter — so communication isn't competing with noise.
Offer objects of reference: a real cup for snack, a nappy for changing, a wellington for garden — concrete things a child can pick up to tell you what they want.
Display a small, well-chosen symbol board of core words — more, finished, help, stop, drink, toilet — at child height and use it yourself.
Sit low, follow the child's gaze, and leave long silences — count to ten in your head before filling the gap, and let them lead.
Comment more than you question: narrate what they're doing rather than firing 'what's that? what colour?' at them.
Keep the same symbols and objects consistent across the room and the team so a child's communication travels with them.
key_questions: What are you showing me — shall we find the symbol for it?
Do you want more, or are you finished?
Can you hand me the thing you'd like?
I'm listening — what do you want to tell me?
Which picture matches what you mean?

impact.text: Children use gesture, pointing, objects and first words to show wants and share attention.
Children take turns in back-and-forth exchanges — vocalising, pausing, waiting for a reply.
Children who are understood by unfamiliar adults grow in confidence to communicate.
Children ask for help and make wants known using words, signs or symbols.
Children respond to familiar words and follow simple instructions in context.

enhancements: A personal communication book or lanyard for a child, built around their real interests and needs and shared with home.
A 'chatterbox' of intriguing objects that prompt comment and questions — a shell, a torch, a wind-up toy.
Photographs of the child's family and pets to talk around, bridging home and setting.
A quiet listening den within the corner — a pop-up tent or draped fabric — for a child who needs even less stimulation.
Core-word symbols repeated at the snack table, the sink and the door so the vocabulary is everywhere, not just here.

playing_exploring: Objects of reference invite handling and exploration, giving pre-verbal children a concrete way to mean something.
The calm space lets children tune in to a quiet, willing adult rather than a busy room.
active_learning: Being genuinely understood — the cup fetched, the sign answered — motivates a child to communicate again.
Children persist at making themselves understood when adults wait rather than rushing in.
creating_thinking: Children make connections between a symbol, an object and a real-world want.
They choose the tool that works — point, sign, photo, word — for the message they need to send.
